rows.description: A child who takes longer with reading calls themselves dumb and stops trying; a single label replaces a specific skill that can be practised.
A wise young adult notices that the very open and the very traditional both hold value. Asks what the other person's preference protects, and avoids labelling curiosity as shallow or caution as dull.

rows.subtype: Feeling like a fraud in a top college [Actor]
rows.description: A student admitted to a prestigious institute believes they got in by luck and that everyone will soon find out; success is discounted while comparison with others is harsh.

rows.subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
rows.description: The person keeps a list of completed work and positive feedback and reads it when doubt spikes. Testing the thought against facts is more effective than trying to feel confident.
A child whose parents respond only to marks feels loved for performance and hides mistakes; the harm is less the standard than the sense that love depends on meeting it.

A wise person sets a time limit, finishes a rough version first and asks what would happen if the work were ninety percent as good. Practising small imperfection builds tolerance, and persistent anxiety warrants support.

rows.subtype: Hiding behind a parent at a party [Actor]
rows.description: A child clings to a parent's leg and refuses to greet anyone; staying away from the scary thing feels like relief, and gentle nearness helps more than pushing.
A teenager replays an embarrassing moment or a harsh remark for days. Harsh self-review feels like accountability but mostly produces shame and avoidance.

rows.subtype: Hiding behind a parent at a party [Actor]
rows.description: A child clings to a parent's leg and refuses to greet anyone; staying away from the scary thing feels like relief, and gentle nearness helps more than pushing.
A child avoids telling a parent about a low grade or a quarrel and delays until it grows. Avoidance makes the eventual talk harder, and a calm parent makes the first admission easier.
A child who stumbles while reading makes a silly face and gets the class laughing with them; the joke keeps control of the moment, though constant clowning can hide worry.

A young adult types haha, lol, emoji or laughing reactions to show amusement or soften a message. The same lol can mean genuine humour, politeness or discomfort, so tone and history matter more than the letters.
